item.title: The Wound Between Friends: Poland, Ukraine, and the Weaponization of History
item.description: Two allies who need each other for survival have begun tearing at an eighty-year-old wound. The wound — the Volhynia massacre — is real. The war over it is manufactured, and the only power that gains from a quarrel between friends is the one at both their gates.

item.title: The Imperial Syndrome Is a Treatable Disease, Not a Russian Gene
item.description: Russians are an imperial people, but imperialism is a socio-cultural condition carried by an inherited cultural code, not by biology. Talk of a Russian "slavery gene" is racial theory in a new coat — and the proof it can be cured is that some Russians have already broken free.

item.title: Russia Cannot Be Reformed Within Its Borders: The Case for Imperial Collapse
item.description: An argument that Russia is an empire pregnant with disintegration, that no reform can make it normal within its present borders, and that only full collapse — including its ethnic Russian core — can finally cure the imperial syndrome.

item.title: The Russian Liberation Army the West Refuses to Build
item.description: There is a way to end this war from within Russia, and it is staring everyone in the face: alongside fully arming Ukraine, build a serious Russian Volunteer Liberation Army from the units already fighting. It fails not for feasibility but for three missing political wills.

item.title: Two Roots of Rus: Why Ukraine Is Not Russia
item.description: "One people" is the founding lie of this war. Ukraine and Russia forked in the Middle Ages from two different roots — Lithuanian Rus and Muscovy — and that civilizational split, not genetics, is why Ukraine is genuinely not Russia.
